source_text: Age jam, qui voles curiositatem melius exercere in negotio salutis tuae, percurre Ecclesias apostolicas, apud quas ipsae adhuc cathedrae Apostolorum suis locis praesident; apud quas ipsae authenticae litterae eorum recitantur, sonantes vocem et repraesentantes faciem uniuscujusque. Proxima est tibi Achaia? habes Corinthum. Si non longe es a Macedonia, habes Philippos, habes Thessalonicenses. Si potes in Asiam tendere, habes Ephesum. Si autem Italiae adjaces, habes Romam, unde nobis quoque auctoritas praesto est. Ista quam felix Ecclesia! cui totam doctrinam Apostoli cum sanguine suo profuderunt; ubi Petrus passioni Dominicae adaequatur; ubi Paulus Joannis exitu coronatur; ubi Apostolus Joannes, posteaquam, in oleum igneum demersus, nihil passus est, in insulam relegatur; videamus quid didicerit, quid docuerit, cum Africanis quoque Ecclesiis contesserarit. Unum Deum novit, creatorem universitatis, et Christum Jesum ex virgine Maria Filium Dei creatoris, et carnis resurrectionem; Legem et Prophetas cum evangelicis et apostolicis litteris miscet, et inde potat fidem; eam aqua signat, Sancto Spiritu vestit, eucharistia pascit, ad martyrium exhortatur, et ita adversus hanc institutionem neminem recipit. Haec est institutio, non dico jam quae futuras haereses praenuntiabat, sed de qua haereses prodierunt. Sed non fuerunt ex illa, ex quo factae sunt adversus illam. Etiam de olivae nucleo mitis et optimae et necessariae asper oleaster oritur; etiam de papavere ficus gratissimae et suavissimae ventosa et vana caprificus exsurgit. Ita et haereses de nostro frutice, non nostro genere; veritatis grano, sed mendacio sylvestres.
pass_a_gloss: Now, if you wish to exercise your curiosity better in the matter of your salvation, run through the apostolic Churches, in which the very chairs of the Apostles still preside in their own places; in which their authentic letters are read, sounding the voice and representing the face of each one. Is Achaia near you? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi, you have the Thessalonians. If you can stretch into Asia, you have Ephesus. If, however, you are adjacent to Italy, you have Rome, from which also authority is at hand for us. What a happy Church is this! To which the Apostles poured out all their doctrine with their own blood; where Peter is equal to the Lord's passion; where Paul is crowned with John's departure; where the Apostle John, after he was immersed in burning oil and suffered nothing, is relegated to an island; let us see what he learned, what he taught, when he was a fellow-soldier with the African Churches. He knows one God, the creator of the universe, and Christ Jesus, the Son of God the creator, from the virgin Mary, and the resurrection of the flesh; He mixes the Law and the Prophets with the evangelical and apostolic letters, and from there he drinks faith; he seals it with water, clothes it with the Holy Spirit, feeds it with the Eucharist, exhorts it to martyrdom, and thus against this institution he receives no one. This is the institution, I do not say now which predicted future heresies, but from which heresies have come forth. But they were not from it, since they were made against it. Also from the nucleus of the olive, a bitter and wild oleaster arises; also from the poppy, a windy and empty caprificus rises; and from the fig, most pleasing and sweetest, a windy and empty caprificus rises. So also heresies from our fruit, not our kind; from the grain of truth, but from the forest of lies.

pass_b_english: So then, if you want to put your curiosity to better use for the sake of your own salvation, make the rounds of the apostolic churches. In them the very chairs of the apostles still preside in their own places, and their authentic letters are read aloud, sounding each voice and representing each face. Is Achaia near you? You have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia, you have Philippi and the Thessalonians. If you can reach Asia, you have Ephesus. But if you border Italy, you have Rome, from which authority is also close at hand for us. What a happy church that is! The apostles poured out their whole teaching there with their own blood; there Peter matches the Lord's passion; there Paul is crowned with John's end; there the apostle John, after he was plunged into burning oil and suffered nothing, was banished to an island. Let us see what he learned and taught when he stood shoulder to shoulder with the African churches. He knows one God, the creator of the universe, and Christ Jesus, the Son of God the creator, born of the virgin Mary, and the resurrection of the flesh. He blends the Law and the Prophets with the gospels and the apostolic writings, and from them he drinks faith; he seals it with water, clothes it with the Holy Spirit, feeds it with the Eucharist, urges it toward martyrdom, and so he admits no one against this institution. This is the institution—not merely one that foretold future heresies, but the one from which heresies have sprung. Yet they did not come from it, because they arose against it. From the kernel of the olive a bitter wild olive also springs; from the poppy a windy, empty caprificus rises; from the fig, most pleasing and sweetest, a windy, empty caprificus rises. So heresies come from our fruit, not our kind; from the grain of truth, but from the forest of lies.

review.notes: Pass A and Pass B both fail to accurately translate the Latin sentence: 'Etiam de olivae nucleo mitis et optimae et necessariae asper oleaster oritur; etiam de papavere ficus gratissimae et suavissimae ventosa et vana caprificus exsurgit.' The Latin describes three distinct comparisons: 1) from the kernel of a mild, best, and necessary olive arises a rough wild olive; 2) from the poppy [arises something]; 3) from the most pleasing and sweetest fig arises a windy and empty caprificus. Both Pass A and Pass B hallucinate a repetition of the 'caprificus' clause for the poppy, which is not in the source. Specifically, Pass A: 'also from the poppy, a windy and empty caprificus rises; and from the fig, most pleasing and sweetest, a windy and empty caprificus rises' and Pass B: 'from the poppy a windy, empty caprificus rises; from the fig, most pleasing and sweetest, a windy, empty caprificus rises' both add 'caprificus' to the poppy clause where the Latin 'de papavere' lacks a subject/predicate, implying the previous structure or a missing element, but certainly does not repeat the caprificus/fig structure twice as written.
reasons: Pass A and Pass B both misinterpret/hallucinate the structure of the final sentences. The Latin 'Etiam de olivae nucleo mitis et optimae et necessariae asper oleaster oritur; etiam de papavere ficus gratissimae et suavissimae ventosa et vana caprificus exsurgit' does not support the repeated 'caprificus' structure found in both English versions. Pass A: 'also from the poppy, a windy and empty caprificus rises; and from the fig, most pleasing and sweetest, a windy and empty caprificus rises' adds content not present in the Latin 'de papavere'.
